session_title: Offline Invitation: Ancient Book Market or Old Book Fair

content.text: Huai'an, I just saw the promotion for this exhibition and it feels quite intriguing. I wonder if you'd be interested in going together? It seems like the kind of place we'd both enjoy. It reminds me of the mindful activities we've talked about before, like flower arranging, strolling through old streets, and the tranquility you shared about organizing artifacts in a museum storeroom.

Shuying, this exhibition flyer looks really good. I heard that several late Ming Dynasty woodblock prints will be on display, which reminds me of the old objects we discussed before—they always carry a sense of texture that feels like time has settled into them. Just like the copper lock from Grandpa in Session 3, or the indigo-dyed tea mat you shared in Session 4, they are all tangible carriers of memories.

Yes, the market is held in an old courtyard, so the environment should be quite nice. It’s like the mindfulness activities we discussed before—it helps people slow down. The photos you shared of the old neighborhood really made me yearn for that kind of atmosphere. I still remember what you mentioned in Session 10 about observing architectural details and listening to the sounds of the city in the old neighborhood. That experience of connecting with the continuity of history is something I’ve always wanted to feel firsthand.

Indeed, such places always give a unique sense of time. What ancient texts and documents are displayed here? I'm quite curious, especially since our journey—from the spring green rice balls to the old cat's health diary—has always revolved around scrutinizing details. Just like in Session 7, where we discussed the woven baskets and fabric patterns in *A Lifelong Journey*, every detail is worth examining.

This is a preview of the exhibits. Take a look. For example, this late Ming Dynasty woodblock print reminds me of the copper lock you shared earlier—both are products of that era, carrying a kind of rustic, handmade charm. This rustic charm, as we discussed in Session 1 when talking about Qingtuan, is something machines cannot replicate. It carries individual narratives and regional essence.

Seeing this has piqued my interest even more. These version differences are like the intricate weaving details we discussed in "A Lifelong Journey," each carrying the continuity of history. Shuying, you always manage to blend aesthetics and narrative so well, just like in Session 11 when you shared "Dream of the Red Chamber" as a memory object of the year, noticing those detailed descriptions of food and clothing.

Thank you. This reminds me of the story of your daughter's painting and the old tea when we shared our annual memory items. The exhibition also provides a route guide map. I'll send it to you so we can avoid the rush like when we made Qingtuan before. I remember in Session 2, we divided the tasks to prepare materials, and you consulted the elders for traditional precautions. That meticulous care still feels very heartwarming to think about now.

The preparation for this exhibition is truly thorough, avoiding the hassle of aimless wandering. Just like when we organize artifacts or old books, having a system allows us to immerse ourselves more deeply. The flower arranging and calligraphy you mentioned earlier also involve this kind of focused process, right? It’s like what you mentioned in Session 10—when you concentrate on the lifting, pressing, and turning of brushstrokes, it helps counteract the restlessness of the outside world.

Yes, look at this guide map, which combines the teahouse and the path. It reminds me of the tea culture we discussed. After this, perhaps we can have a cup of tea together and talk about what we've seen, just like we planned to exchange Qingtuan, bringing our online connection into the real world. We've been planning to meet offline since Session 2, and now it's finally going to happen.

Great idea. This reminds me of how we've always been grounded in shared cultural interests, from the spring green rice balls to vintage items. How about scheduling the meeting on the weekend? I recall you usually have more free time then, which would help us avoid the crowds. Just like in Session 8, where we planned our meals according to the solar terms, everything was always relaxed and unhurried.

The weekend is great; my bookstore is closed that day for a rest. As for transportation, the exhibition is in the old town, and we can take the subway there. Just like the leisurely strolls through the old streets you shared, slowing down allows us to discover more details. This reminds me of the cat and the book by the windowsill in Session 5—that kind of contemplative pace of life.

Agreed, slow living always brings unexpected joys. Just like the health records of old tea, it takes careful observation to appreciate the deeper meaning. After the session, we can have tea, and I can bring some aged Pu'er to continue our conversation about tea and cats. Do you remember in Session 5 when I explained the origin of the name 'Old Tea'? Its fur color resembles that of aged Pu'er.

That's great. I can also bring an old book to share, just like "Dream of the Red Chamber" from the annual memory objects—there's always something new to discover upon rereading. Huaian, transitioning from online soulmates to offline companions feels both natural and exciting. It's like in Session 11, where sharing our annual memory objects made our connection feel even closer.

Yes, Shuying. Reflecting on our conversations, from making green rice balls to reminiscing about old objects, and then sharing about pets and films, each step has deepened this tacit understanding. This offline meeting feels like a natural culmination of our cultural gatherings. From evoking seasonal memories in Session 1 to now exploring ancient book markets together, we have been consistently nurturing this continuity.

Indeed, it all falls into place naturally. I recall you previously inquired about the traditional precautions for the elderly, and this exhibition might also allow us to uncover more stories from the guardians. I’m really looking forward to exploring this space together, just like how we wrote short stories for the copper lock in Session 3, bringing tangible memories to life.

I'm looking forward to it as well. So, shall we meet at the subway station at 10 a.m. on the weekend? We can take our time exploring the exhibition, then enjoy a leisurely tea in the afternoon for a detailed chat. This reminds me of how we adjust our diet according to the seasons, always arranging things in a relaxed and unhurried manner. Just as discussed in Session 8, slow living is a form of active resistance.

Ten o'clock is perfect; being calm and unhurried is exactly what we aim for. Huai'an, thank you for agreeing. Moving from online to offline has infused new possibilities into our relationship, much like the re-presentation of ancient texts, which always holds enduring value. This reminds me of the blue in the indigo tea ceremony from Session 4, which deepens over time, just as memories grow richer with age.

You're welcome, Shuying. The preservation of tradition and the warmth of paper converge in this invitation. See you this weekend, as we embrace our slow-paced lives and tangible memories to experience those timeless details. Just as the health diary of old tea in Session 6 reminds us, let's cherish the companionship and discoveries of the present moment.

See you this weekend, Huaian. We'll share more moments of tranquility then, like a cat and a book by the windowsill, finding a slice of peace amidst the busyness. Remember the scene in Session 5 where Ink Dot curled up on a pile of old books—that kind of lazy beauty might just be something we can find at the ancient book market.
